Although the model is specifically calibrated for an envisioned Independent System Operator of New England (ISO-NE) system, methods and results are generalizable to other bulk power systems integrating increasing shares of EVMC. By combining these improvements over current practice with no-foresight and perfect-foresight forecast bracketing of TOU and RTP EVMC performance, this study provides a realistic accounting of how well price-responsive EVMC dispatch mechanisms compare to DLC across a wide range of participation rates in an envisioned future power system with high renewable energy shares. 3 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Methods This study adjusts and extends the workflow of Hale et al. (2022a) to estimate the value of perfect-foresight forecasts of price-responsive EVMC, compared to both no-foresight forecasts of price-responsive EVMC and a low-error DLC formulation, in a production cost model. Sections 2.1 to 2.4 present methods developed in the previous study as needed to understand this study’s results. The production cost modeling implementation, which differs in some ways from that of Hale et al. (2022a), is described in Section 2.5. Section 2.6 presents our scenario framework. Additional methodological information is available in Hale et al. (2022a) and in Appendix A and Appendix B. 2.1 Study Setting We examine EVMC simulated in a production cost model of an envisioned ISO-NE 2038 bulk power system derived from the Interconnections Seam Study (SEAMS) (Bloom et al. 2022). We chose ISO-NE as our study region because it is a well-defined, moderately sized system that is relatively easy to isolate from the rest of the Eastern Interconnection and Quebec by fixing hourly imports and exports. In the 2038 scenario selected from SEAMS, 84% of ISO-NE within- system generation is sourced from wind, solar, biomass, hydropower, and nuclear generators. As in Bloom et al. (2022) and Hale et al. (2022a), production cost modeling is nodal and uses the commercial PLEXOS software (Energy Exemplar n.d.). We add electric LDV load for 2038 based on the “All LDV Sales EV by 2035” scenario described by Yip et al. (2023), which captures current county-level heterogeneity in EV ownership and adoption and then transitions county-level LDV EV sales shares to 100% by 2035 at rates aligned with state and federal policy goals. As described by Yip et al. (2023), the TEMPOTM model creates realistic sample vehicle mobility demand data by modeling household vehicle adoption considering county-specific demographics, vehicle registrations, and weather and assigning weekly mobility demand profiles and sample weights that are also consistent with those variables. For this study, TEMPO also provides a vehicle-level weekly EV charging time series consistent with the weekly mobility demand profiles using different charging strategies.
